plan.title: Calm Before You Speak: Handling Presentation Anxiety
plan.description: A practical guide to performance anxiety before presentations: why your body reacts the way it does, breathing and preparation techniques that help, and when to talk to a professional. This is general information, not medical advice.

beats.narration: Your heart pounds. Your hands shake. Your mind goes blank. And yet nothing is attacking you. It is just a room full of people, waiting for you to talk.

props.alt: people waiting in a presentation room

beats.chapter: Why your body panics before you speak

beats.narration: Here is what happens. Your brain sounds an alarm. That releases adrenaline. And adrenaline leaves your body ready to act, as if you had to fight or run.
This fight or flight response helped early humans survive real danger. The problem is that your brain can't always tell a wild animal from an audience watching you.
Adrenaline explains the symptoms. A faster heartbeat. Quick, shallow breathing. Sweating. Shaky hands. A dry mouth. Each one is your body preparing for action.
Feeling judged is an especially strong trigger. We are social animals, so being negatively evaluated by others registers in the brain as a threat. That is why presentations feel so dangerous.

props.text: Feeling judged makes the brain sound the alarm.

beats.narration: Here is a useful twist. Nerves and excitement feel physically almost the same: racing heart, buzzing energy. So you can try reading that feeling as energy, not fear.
So some nervousness is normal. It can even sharpen your focus. Most speakers feel it, which means you are not alone, and nothing is wrong with you.

props.alt: people speaking in front of audiences

beats.narration: Now for the good part: you can send your body a calmer signal. The simplest way is your breath. Slow breathing, with a longer exhale, helps settle the alarm.

props.text: Make the exhale longer than the inhale.

beats.chapter: Breathing and preparation that actually help

beats.narration: Here is how. Breathe in through your nose for a comfortable count. Then breathe out slowly through your mouth for a longer count. Repeat for a few rounds.
Try it gently, without forcing. If you feel dizzy or strained, ease off. Slow exhales nudge the body toward rest and digest, which is the opposite of panic.

props.alt: relaxed woman taking a deep breath

beats.narration: To check you are breathing low, try belly breathing. Rest a hand on your stomach. When you inhale, that hand should rise. Your chest stays quieter.

props.alt: person with hand on belly breathing

beats.narration: Breathing calms the moment. Preparation shrinks the fear. Practise aloud, ideally in the real room or in front of a friend, so the situation already feels familiar.

image_queries: practicing presentation in front of friend
props.alt: rehearsing a presentation in a real room

beats.narration: Know your opening lines especially well, because the first moments are the hardest. Once you are past them, the words tend to flow.
On the day, arrive early. Drink some water. And reframe the feeling: that racing heart is not only fear, it can be excitement. Tell yourself, I am excited.
Most nerves fade once you start speaking, or once the event is over. But what if the fear doesn't fade? What if it follows you for weeks?

props.title: When nerves need more support
props.subtitle: Normal nerves fade. Constant fear deserves attention.

beats.narration: Some anxiety is normal and even helpful. It sharpens attention and effort. It is worth seeking help when anxiety is intense, constant, or keeps coming back.
Signs it may be time to talk to someone: avoiding presentations, work or school because of fear. Dread for weeks. Panic attacks. Poor sleep. Or losing confidence.
Some signs are urgent. Chest pain, trouble breathing that does not ease, or thoughts of harming yourself. Contact emergency services or a crisis line right away. Support exists, and you deserve it.

props.heading: Get urgent care for
items: Trouble breathing that does not ease

beats.narration: A doctor or therapist can help. Cognitive behavioural therapy is commonly used for anxiety. It helps you spot fearful thoughts, then practise speaking in small, gradual steps.
This is general information, not medical advice. For your own situation, speak to a doctor or mental health professional. You do not have to wait until it feels unbearable.

props.alt: A person talking with a therapist

beats.narration: So remember: your body is trying to help. Slow your exhale. Practise out loud. And if fear is running your life, ask for support. That is your next step.

props.text: Slow your exhale. Practise out loud. Ask for support.
